children: The internet is awash in videos created by self-styled financial influencers peddling investment strategies to an increasingly online audience eager for wisdom. Yet nearly all of them lack the qualifications considered necessary for providing financial advice, a new analysis finds.
An analysis of more than 1,700 English-language postings on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube found that just 2.2% of the content creators had "relevant demonstrable financial qualifications."

Those videos had been viewed more than 692 million times, but Legalaes, the financial licensing consultancy that published the research, determined that 29% were misleading. The videos that Legalaes deemed misleading had an average of 555,547 views, while nonmisleading videos averaged 326,170 views.
"This is alarming because finance and investment content have a direct impact on a person's financial stability," the company says.

Legalaes branded a video misleading if it promoted a paid product or service, projected specific or guaranteed returns, or provided harmful or inaccurate advice. The analysis found that only 1.9% of the social-media videos contained potentially damaging information, while 1.1% offered inaccurate advice.

"Note that a video can be both accurate and misleading if it provides accurate advice but has one or more risk signals," Legalaes says. "Educational content grounded in established investment principles and sound financial advice is misleading if it also promotes a paid product or service, suggests specific return/outcome, recommends a specific investment amount, or uses guaranteed-return language."

Looking at the individual platforms, researchers found that nearly 42% of the finfluencer videos they analyzed on YouTube were misleading. Of the finfluencer videos on Instagram, nearly 27% were deemed misleading. The researchers identified just over 23% of the videos on Facebook they analyzed as misleading, and an even 23% of the TikTok videos they considered.

Legalaes found that 5.1% of the finfluencers on YouTube had relevant qualifications to be offering advice, well ahead of the other platforms, where the percentages ranged from 1.6% on Instagram to 1% on Facebook and 0.7% on TikTok. YouTube was also the platform most likely to host content by paid promoters.

Legalaes found that just under 12% of the videos it analyzed included disclaimers either in the video itself or on the creator's profile and urged investors to be cautious when viewing content posted by finfluencers and to research their qualifications.

"There's plenty of financial content on social-media platforms, but following financial advice on social media can put retail investors and their hard-earned money at risk," the company says. "[M]uch financial content on social media seems to have been created to induce retail investors into acting, without full transparency on possible adverse consequences, to draw customers into marketing funnels to generate leads and sales."
